# Jenna Ammerall — Product Designer

> Making products make sense. As a senior product designer with nine years at
> Microsoft and Meta, Jenna gets to the root of the problem, defines the behaviors,
> and builds the frameworks teams need to carry those decisions across
> products—so everything moves as one. Seattle-based. Focus areas: design systems,
> accessibility, interaction design, platform and information architecture.
> Site: https://ammerallj.design/

Contact: ammerallj@gmail.com · https://www.linkedin.com/in/ammerallj/

## Selected work

- [Shaping Accessibility Across Products](https://ammerallj.design/work/accessibility.html): Meta, Risk Areas / Accessibility, December 2023–July 2026. Design Lead across product systems, interaction design, and AI strategy. Accessibility had relied on specialists catching issues late in development; the European Accessibility Act made it business-critical, and reviewing after the fact couldn't keep up with AI-accelerated build cycles. The deeper problem: a standard only becomes real when people can find it, apply it, verify it, and trust it—and at Meta's scale, none of that happened on its own. What changed: product teams could apply the accessibility standard during design and build, with a playbook that translated 29 requirements into 23 practical topics organized around the decisions teams were already making; accessibility review stopped being a manual bottleneck, as shared workflows reduced the manual coordination required across program managers, reviewers, and product teams, while automated checks cut a recurring 3–5 hour review to effectively zero per wave and a separate submission workflow saved 1,711 hours; product teams could go from an accessibility question to the guidance that applied without searching through 200+ pages, reducing deprecated results from 25% to zero; people could find accessibility support in one place for the first time, as a needs-based model became a customer-facing experience bringing 30+ features and 45 Help Center articles into a single path on meta.com. Full case study is confidential; the public destination is live at https://www.meta.com/accessibility/

- [Creating Continuity Across Messaging](https://ammerallj.design/work/messaging.html): Meta, Facebook Messaging, April–December 2023. Design Lead across interaction design and product strategy. On Facebook, private sharing is how conversations start—a Reel or listing sent to one person—but continuing meant replying in Messenger, and entry points designed in isolation made conversations less predictable. Impact: standardized in-app messaging across Facebook surfaces with a reusable interaction model that continued guiding rollout after handoff; informed a rollout addressing ~144M monthly switches from Facebook to Messenger; experimentation validated a key part of the interaction model at +21.9% thread opens on iOS and +27.1% on Android with neutral topline metrics. Scope note: ownership was localized to Jenna's org and leadership, not Meta's messaging ecosystem. Full case study is confidential.

- [Giving Components an Identity](https://ammerallj.design/work/microsoft-loop.html): Microsoft, Loop, May 2020–March 2022. UX Designer across interaction, platform, and visual design. Microsoft Loop introduced live components that could move across Microsoft 365; the hard part was making one read as the same live thing in every app it landed in. Impact: designed the Loop control—the persistent interaction model for identity, sharing, and collaboration—patented as "Interactive user interface controls for shared dynamic objects" (US 12,277,305); shipped Microsoft's first Loop components into Teams, enabling live collaborative tables, lists, agendas, and action items that stayed synchronized wherever they were shared (the Fluid work that became Microsoft Loop, debuting at Ignite 2021); Microsoft's public developer documentation now specifies the header and border that mark a Loop component as live and portable.

- [Helping People Navigate Communities](https://ammerallj.design/work/facebook-groups.html): Meta, Facebook Groups, March 2022–April 2023. Product Designer across interaction design, design systems, and design quality. Most people on Facebook belong to at least 15 active groups and more than 100 million join one every day; people needed clearer ways to navigate between communities without losing context. Impact: moved topline engagement on a mature consumer surface roughly a quarter-percent; raised design-system adoption across Facebook Groups past 80%, cutting inconsistency and recurring design debt across iOS and Android; held the quality bar with 17 implementation reviews with engineering and 200+ UI issues resolved.
